text: End of course test, track two. Good morning and welcome to this morning's podcast, The Rise of the Social Seniors. I'm joined today by psychologist Dr Annika Andrews. So the elderly are taking over social media websites like Facebook and Twitter, Dr Andrews. Good morning, Charlie. I wouldn't say taking over exactly, but they are starting to use smartphones and tablets in record numbers. But surely social media is a little challenging for older people. Wouldn't they be better off leaving all that to the younger generation? Charlie, why on earth would you suggest that? A quarter of the over 75s use tablets and why shouldn't they? There are huge cognitive and mental health benefits to this growing trend. Yes, the older generation certainly enjoy online brain training quizzes and crosswords. That's not really what I was referring to. What I'm talking about are things like setting up a social media account. Think about it, Charlie. Learning a new skill can be challenging. For example, you need to focus. You need to navigate in an unknown world. You need to acquire new knowledge to do things like set up a profile, upload a photograph or post a status update. For someone born in 1945, this might stimulate the brain in the same way as going to school or learning to speak a new language. If I felt like I had to go back to school, I don't think I'd bother. Seriously though, it might be an idea if they did go back, I mean to college or do some sort of computer training course. It's interesting you say that. Did you know that a UK study has shown that using social media actually improves the health of senior citizens? In the study, 100 people aged over 65 were studied over a period of two years. Some received computer training, for example on how to use the internet, while the other group did not. Those who surfed the web experienced an improvement in their mental and physical abilities. In contrast, these abilities declined steadily for the other group. That's remarkable. I hadn't realised elderly people were so confident online. Don't misunderstand me, Charlie. I didn't say they were all confident. While the older generation are increasingly active online, some do lack online confidence. A fifth of over 65s do not describe themselves as confident online. This is particularly the case when managing personal data. For instance, one in five internet users over the age of 65 said they were not confident about managing passwords and other sensitive data, more worryingly perhaps, 16% of users over 55 admitted to never considering the privacy of their online posts. That is the largest percentage for any age group. What about getting guidance from grandchildren about online safety? I guess that might work if they have grandchildren that they see face to face or online on a regular basis, but we need to think about a more practical approach. Some websites offer practical information, but that's only helpful if people know it's there and how to find it. Yes, websites can be difficult to understand when they're describing something technical. So how do you think the issue of online safety should be approached? In my view, the only answer is a more proactive approach, where agencies step in to provide support if relatives are unable to do so for whatever reason, especially as we are seeing more cybercrime daily that targets elderly people. That way, the older generation can continue to enjoy the health benefits with confidence. Thank you, Dr Andrews. Cybercrime will be the topic of our podcast next week. For now, that's all we have time for. Thank you.
